analysis.one_liner: Bans political action committees from spending money in federal elections.
analysis.headline: The bill to ban PAC contributions in federal elections drew no cosponsors and died in committee without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend federal election law to bar political action committees — committees set up by corporations, unions, trade groups, and other organizations — from giving money to federal candidates or spending on their elections. It would also limit House candidates to raising no more than 20 percent of their total contributions from sources outside their state, such as donors from other states. Candidate committees and political party committees would keep their current abilities under the bill.
analysis.who_benefits: Voters would benefit from reduced direct influence of organized-money committees over federal elections, since candidates would have to rely more on individual donors, including constituents, and House candidates would have to draw most of their money from people who actually live in their state.

how_it_helps.text: Bans political action committees from making contributions, soliciting or receiving contributions, or making expenditures to influence federal elections [S3].
Restricts House candidates so that no more than 20 percent of total contributions accepted may come from sources other than individual residents of the candidate's state [S3].
Applies to federal elections held after December 31, 1998 [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Political action committees funded by corporations, unions, and trade associations would lose their direct channel of giving to federal candidates, and House members who relied heavily on PAC money and out-of-state donors would have to rebuild their fundraising around individual constituents.

drawbacks.text: The ban exempts candidate committees and national, state, local, and district party committees, so large sums could still flow through party committees rather than disappearing [S3].
A widely recognized trade-off of PAC bans is that organized money can shift toward less transparent channels, such as party soft money and independent expenditures, which the bill does not address.
The 20 percent in-state cap could disadvantage candidates whose states have fewer wealthy individual donors, since it limits their ability to fund a campaign from national individual donors.
Contributions and spending restrictions of this kind raise First Amendment free-speech objections that courts weigh in campaign finance cases, though the bill text itself does not address them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets the most direct and traceable route by which organized special interests — corporate, union, and trade-association PACs — fund federal candidates, and the in-state rule pushes House candidates toward their own constituents. Its main weaknesses are the carve-out for party committees, which could simply relocate the money, and the fact that a PAC-only ban leaves independent spending untouched. On balance it is a genuine but incomplete piece of campaign finance reform, and its lack of a single cosponsor signaled it was going nowhere.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Administration committee, which took no action on it, and it died there when the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Bill Archer introduced the bill on January 6, 1999 [S1, S5].
It was referred the same day to the House Committee on House Administration [S5, S1].
No further action was taken, and no cosponsors ever joined the bill [S4, S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Political action committees and the corporate, union, and trade-association interests behind them kept their contribution channel to federal candidates intact, and officeholders kept their existing fundraising base.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: PACs and the interests funding them

for.name: Rep. Bill Archer
for.role: House Ways and Means Committee chairman; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, and never gained a cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on House Administration
against.role: Committee of referral; the bill's only referral
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and never reported it out or scheduled any action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party, so no partisan split ever formed around it.

industries.industry: Political action committees (corporate, union, and trade-association PACs)
industries.note: PACs are the organized-money committees through which businesses, unions, and trade groups give directly to federal candidates; the bill would eliminate that channel entirely. Reducing it narrows a tool these interests use to gain access and influence over officeholders.

Incumbents raise heavily from PACs and out-of-state donors, so the bill would force them to retool their fundraising around in-state individual donors. Nothing in the record shows officeholders acted on the bill either way.

The bill explicitly exempts national, state, local, and district party committees from the PAC ban, leaving party committees as a permitted channel for organized contributions while shutting down PACs.
